study.title: Psalm 26 Integrity before God, separation from evil and trust to praise
study.overview: This psalm presents David asking God to judge his cause and examine his life. The central point is not a moral self-reliance, but the confidence that his conduct, his attachment to the truth of God and his distance from the company of the wicked show sincerity before the Lord. At the same time, the psalm ends with dependence on divine mercy: the psalmist wants to remain on a safe way and praise God publicly.

outline.title: I appeal to divine judgment and openness to examination
outline.explanation: David asks the Lord for justice on the basis of his integrity and invites God to test his interior. He states that his life has been marked by trust in the Lord, by divine truth as a constant reference and by a habitual disposition to walk according to that truth.

outline.title: Separation of evil and love for the presence of God
outline.explanation: The psalmist declares that he avoids coexistence with deceptive and perverse people. In contrast, he speaks of symbolic purity, approaching the altar and love for the house of God, where the glory of the Lord dwells, indicating pleasure in divine ordinances and desire to worship.

outline.title: Request for deliverance, mercy and firmness to praise
outline.explanation: He asks that his soul be placed not with sinners and violent, whose life is marked by evil intention and corruption. Conclusing by reaffirming his integrity, supplicating deliverance and mercy, and expressing assurance that his steps are in a firm place to praise the Lord in the congregation.

study.context: The notes suggest that this psalm may have been written in time of persecution and false accusations, possibly during the opposition of Saul and his group. This identification is presented by commentators as likely, not as textual certainty. There is also mention of reading that sees the psalm in association with the context of exile, but without sufficient evidence to state this safely. The text, in any case, depicts someone under suspicion that appeals directly to God's judgment.
study.theology: The psalm unites moral integrity, divine examination and worship. The righteousness asked of God is not based on absolute impeccability, but on the sincerity of a life that seeks to walk in truth, to reject evil and to love the presence of the Lord. There is here a theology of practical holiness: whoever belongs to God does not want to participate in the corruption of the wicked or to be confused with his ways. At the same time, the psalmist does not trust himself as the final foundation; he supplicates mercy and deliverance. The outcome shows that the firmness of the righteous comes from the Lord, and that the proper response to the grace received is public praise in the assembly.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist submits to the divine examination especially as to his character and his devotion; in 26:3, the truth of God becomes only part of character through habitual commitment.
David stands under a solemn test before God and his own conscience, claiming his integrity and sincere affection for the Lord's ordinances.
The psalmist asks that God not to bring together his soul with sinners, for he does not love their company or follow his practices.

questions: Is my trust really in the Lord, or in my own appearance of righteousness?
Is there any coexistence, habit or influence that brings me closer to the path of the wicked and weakens my devotion?
Am I seeking the presence of God and public praise with sincerity, or just preserving a religious image?
study.practice: Practice an examination prayer before God: ask him to reveal motivations, affections, and choices. Then identify a concrete area in which you need to depart from corrupting influences and a concrete practice of devotion that needs to be strengthened, such as biblical reading, prayer or faithful participation in the congregation. Finally, transform the security that God gives into visible praise, not just in private words.
study.uncertainty: The notes only allow to affirm as likely the connection of the psalm with persecution and false accusations, especially in the period of Saul, and do not definitively confirm this. It is also not possible to determine with certainty, from these notes, whether the mention of 26:12 should be read mainly as an image of salvation, stability or both; the commentators approach these ideas in different ways.
